rewrites.summary:
Madagascar's trans visitors get legality without protection. Same-sex conduct between adults is legal from age 21 under the Penal Code, but the age of consent is unequal: same-sex acts involving someone under 21 remain offences, with Penal Code Article 331 attaching an indecent-assault band of five to ten years' imprisonment. There is no anti-discrimination law, no legal gender recognition, and no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, so a trans traveller — alone or with a partner — holds no local status and no named protection.

Practical safety is the dominant concern: LGBT people must hide their lives to keep jobs and live in peace, and there is no visible community outside the capital, Antananarivo. No police targeting pattern is documented, and the government has rejected UN recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech, so no protection is in prospect.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Regional context colours — but does not set — the assessment: by July 2020 around 22 of 53 African states across the region had decriminalised same-sex conduct, and Madagascar's confinement of legality to adults over 21 sits at the stricter end of that pattern. In a fourth international review (January 2025, carrying 235 recommendations) the government rejected recommendations on anti-LGBT violence, hate speech and the age of consent — six local organisations protested that refusing to act endorses impunity and condones violence.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Residents face the same closed-door social pressure the visitor assessments describe: LGBT people must hide their lives to keep jobs and live in peace, developing their own networks and coded language, and there is no visible community outside the capital, Antananarivo.

A 2011 human-rights report documented societal discrimination and violence against women, persons with disabilities, and the LGBT community. Resident legal avenues are equally bare: no civil marriage or adoption for same-sex couples, and no legal gender recognition.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Thin data; legal but closeted profile. No source addresses border-screening, document handling, or passport-marker practice for trans visitors, and no police targeting pattern is documented either way — the absence of a documented pattern is not proof of safety. The legal baseline rests on a 2020 decriminalisation overview, a December 2023 guide, and a 2011 human-rights report describing a post-coup period.

blindSourceSummaries: News report (Aug 2024): although same-sex conduct is not illegal, it is widely considered socially unacceptable; many hide their lives to keep jobs and live in peace, developing their own networks and coded language.
Government human-rights report (2011): documents societal discrimination and violence against women, persons with disabilities, and the LGBT community.

Broadcaster overview (July 2020): same-sex activity is legal only for adults of 21 and older; same-sex acts involving younger partners remain offences; no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions; many nations in the region had moved to decriminalise.

Travel guide (December 2023): same-sex activity is legal for adults over 21 but LGBT people face discrimination and lack civic rights such as marriage and adoption; the legal framework lags other nations.

News report (17 July 2025): in a fourth international review (January 2025) the government rejected recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent; six local organisations protested.

Refugee-law resource: the criminal code sets a different age of consent for same-sex acts, with an indecent-assault band of five to ten years' imprisonment; documents general societal discrimination against LGBT people, government protection capacity, case law and supporting organisations.
rewrites.notes: Four-field split of country:MDG from current_summary plus the six source claims. Visitor-relevant law and safety (legality from 21 with the unequal consent band, no LGR, no anti-discrimination law, no marriage recognition, hide-to-work safety, no police pattern, rejected recommendations) to summary; regional decriminalisation comparison and the UPR-process detail with the organisations' protest to tangentialFactors; resident-facing hide/work/coded-language facts, the 2011 discrimination-and-violence report and the resident legal-avenue gap to localsOnly; thin-data, unverified border-screening/document practice and source-vintage caveats to outOfScopeNotes. current_tangential and current_localsOnly were empty in the batch; current_outOfScope preserved and expanded.
